solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique, linked answer split by the grid); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Throbs wildly holding club's top dish

indicators.note: holding says the scrambled letters wrap round the next piece
wildly says the letters of throbs are thrown about into a new order
top here means the first letter of the word club's

explanation.surface: Something pulses madly while gripping the best dish a club serves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wildly' turns THROBS into BORSHT, and 'holding' puts C, the 'top' of club's, inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Borscht is an Eastern European beetroot soup, so it is a dish served at table.

clue.text: He has one win — no-one explained racing starts

indicators.note: starts asks for the opening letter of each of the five words before it

explanation.surface: A racing commentator says someone has one win, though nobody explained how.
explanation.walkthrough: 'starts' takes the first letters of one, win, no-one, explained and racing.
explanation.definitionFit: The definition reads as a description: a person who has something possesses it, the proprietor.

clue.text: Where 21 might have ended up if he hadn't uncovered it?

definitions.text: Where 21 might have ended up if he hadn't uncovered it?

parts.words: Where 21 might have ended up if he hadn't uncovered it?
parts.note: Had he not, he might have ended up buried in a grave ... there

explanation.surface: A question about where the king would have finished had he missed something.
explanation.walkthrough: The 1415 conspiracy is named after the port city on England's south coast, and 'plot' also means a burial place, so both senses meet in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1415 conspiracy to kill Henry V is known by the name of the port where it was uncovered.

indicators.note: in says the scrambled letters go inside the hero's surname

parts.note: Ben-Hur is the title character of the famous novel and film, so Ben leads to his surname

indicators.note: waving means the letters of the flare are moved about, as a flare flickers

parts.note: the blog parses this as the word flare; the printed fare lacks the L

explanation.surface: A man named Ben waves food at a place the king captured.
explanation.walkthrough: Ben-Hur, the hero of the novel and film, gives his surname. The clue as held reads 'fare', which lacks the L the anagram needs; the blog reads it as 'flare'.
explanation.definitionFit: Harfleur is the Normandy port that Henry V besieged and took in 1415 before marching on to battle.

clue.text: 18, 5 for example, told to treasure ecstasy

indicators.note: told signals that the pieces are spoken and their sound gives the answer

parts.note: to treasure something is to love it; E is the street abbreviation for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: A famous actor is said to cherish a drug.
explanation.walkthrough: Spoken together, LOVE and E sound like the answer. 18, 5 is Laurence Olivier, an actor, and luvvie is the British slang word for an actor, often a gushing one.
explanation.definitionFit: Luvvie is British slang for an actor, especially an affected one, and Olivier is an example.

indicators.note: small says the word is cut short, losing its end

parts.note: volume is the amount of space something takes up

explanation.surface: An emblem with wings fits into a tiny area.
explanation.walkthrough: 'small' shortens VOLUME to its first three letters, the usual abbreviation. In heraldry a vol is a pair of wings joined at the base.
explanation.definitionFit: In heraldry a vol is a charge showing two wings joined together, a winged emblem on a shield.

clue.text: A nice pure stew for gourmet

indicators.note: stew means the letters are mixed together like ingredients in a pot

explanation.surface: A tasty, wholesome stew suits a food lover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stew' looks like the dish the gourmet eats, but it is the instruction to rearrange A NICE PURE.
explanation.definitionFit: An epicurean is a person devoted to refined food and drink, the same as a gourmet.

clue.text: Those sent after 16 would have been miserable protection

definitions.text: Those sent after 16 would have been miserable protection

parts.words: Those sent after 16 would have been miserable protection
parts.note: after their defeat at Agincourt the French soldiers' letters home would have been miserable; the phrase is also British slang for condoms, a form of protection

explanation.surface: The messages sent home after a battle would have offered poor comfort.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer, a British slang name for condoms, is read literally as letters written by the French after Agincourt.
explanation.definitionFit: Read literally, the phrase means letters from the French; in British slang it means condoms, a kind of protection.

clue.text: Investigator heard when choir are content

indicators.note: heard says that those inner letters, spoken, give the answer
content means what is held inside the phrase, the letters within its outer ends

explanation.surface: A detective listens while the singers are satisfied.
explanation.walkthrough: 'content' takes ENCHOIRAR from inside 'when choir are'; 'heard' says that run, spoken as 'en-quire-er', gives the answer. 'content' looks like happy, but it means the contents.
explanation.definitionFit: An enquirer is a person who asks questions to find something out, an investigator.

clue.text: Physio lavishly hosts return of 21's in-laws

indicators.note: return of says the letters held there are read backwards
hosts says the phrase holds the answer's letters inside it, like guests

explanation.surface: A physiotherapist generously entertains returning relatives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hosts' finds SIOLAV inside 'Physio lavishly' and 'return of' turns it round. Henry V married Catherine of Valois, so the French royal house were his in-laws.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry V married Catherine of Valois, so the French royal house of that name were his in-laws.

definitions.meaning: knowing in the sense of sly or roguish
chief in the sense of principal

explanation.definitionFit: Arch means both playfully knowing, as of a smile, and chief, as in arch-rival.

indicators.note: starter here means the first letter of the word lovely
Turn tells you to rearrange the letters that follow, as if turning them over

explanation.surface: A cook is told to make dried beans into a pleasant first course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn' rearranges PULSE, INTO and L, the 'starter' of lovely. The whole clue also describes the dish: a pulse turned into a starter.
explanation.definitionFit: Lentils are a pulse, and soup made from them is a common first course, so the whole clue describes it.

parts.note: drab read upwards in a down clue gives bard, the common name for this playwright, who wrote the play Henry V

explanation.surface: Someone describes a dull outfit as a quotation from a play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'get-up' says drab is read upwards in this down entry, giving BARD. The Bard is the usual nickname for the playwright, who wrote Henry V, but the clue gives only the nickname, not the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The playwright, called the Bard, wrote the history play Henry V about the king.

clue.text: Ordered night fiers to cover unsatisfactory smears

parts.note: bad is an old past tense of bid, so it can mean ordered

indicators.note: to cover says the moths sit round the next letter

parts.note: moths are insects that fly at night (fiers is how the clue is held, for fliers)
U is a grade for unsatisfactory, as on a school report

explanation.surface: Someone told insects of the night to blanket a poor result.
explanation.walkthrough: Bad is an archaic past tense of bid, so 'Ordered' fits. U as 'unsatisfactory' is a grade on some report cards; 'fiers' is the clue as held, for fliers.
explanation.definitionFit: To badmouth someone is to criticise them unfairly, the same as smearing their name.

indicators.note: reproduced means the letters are produced again in a different order

explanation.surface: A theatre company says its own performance restaged the king's victory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reproduced' rearranges OUR ACTING. Agincourt, 1415, was Henry V's great victory over the French.
explanation.definitionFit: Agincourt was the battle of 1415 where Henry V's army defeated the French, his greatest victory.

clue.text: Quiz showmen, maybe, from board tables

parts.note: a board is a panel, as in a board of directors or of wood
tables are lists, as in a league table or tables of figures

explanation.surface: Games show hosts are perhaps seated at the boardroom table.
explanation.walkthrough: On a quiz show the celebrity guests who answer the questions are the panellists, so 'showmen, maybe' is fair.
explanation.definitionFit: Panellists are the guests on a quiz show's panel, showmen of a sort.

parts.note: continuing from the previous clue, this actor's film of Henry V was a triumph

explanation.surface: The ellipsis carries on from the clue before: this man's portrayal of the king was a triumph too.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links back to 16, so 'one' means a triumph: the British actor's 1944 film of Henry V was hailed as a triumph.
explanation.definitionFit: The great British actor directed and starred in the 1944 film of Henry V, a critical triumph.

clue.text: A million? A grand? Almost worthless!

definitions.meaning: at ten pounds for each penny, a thousand pounds becomes a million
the phrase means very common and so of little value

explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means so plentiful as to be almost worthless; literally ten for each penny turns a thousand into a million.

clue.text: Inductance with volts DC — years since his power start-up

definitions.text: DC — years since his power start-up

parts.note: the henry is the SI unit of electrical inductance
V is the symbol for volts

explanation.surface: An electrical spec mixes units with direct current.
explanation.walkthrough: DC looks like direct current, but it is Roman 600: the clue's year was 600 years after Henry V took the throne in 1413.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry V became king in 1413, six hundred years (Roman DC) before the puzzle appeared.

clue.text: Splitter of wood on heavenly drink, we hear

indicators.note: we hear says the words before it are spoken, and their sound gives the answer

parts.note: teak is a hardwood; taken as written; nectar is the drink of the gods in Greek myth

explanation.surface: A tool for splitting timber sits on a celestial beverage.
explanation.walkthrough: Spoken quickly, TEAK ON NECTAR sounds like the answer. 'Splitter of wood' looks like an axe, but 'Splitter' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A T-connector is a fitting that divides one pipe or cable into two branches, so it splits a line.

parts.note: O is round in shape
a zone is an area

explanation.surface: A guard is placed around a district.
explanation.walkthrough: The ozone layer protects the Earth by absorbing ultraviolet light from the sun.
explanation.definitionFit: The ozone layer shields the Earth from the sun's ultraviolet radiation, so it is a form of protection.

parts.note: Hun is an old derogatory nickname for a German
Ger is the abbreviation for German

explanation.surface: A pair of German people feel a pain.
explanation.walkthrough: One word gives both pieces: HUN, a wartime slang term for a German, and GER, the abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: To hunger is to ache or long for something, as in hunger for success.

indicators.note: evens out says the even-numbered letters are removed, leaving the odd ones

explanation.surface: A hairdressing product smooths away grey hair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'evens out' drops the 2nd, 4th and 6th letters of greyly (R, Y, Y), leaving the 1st, 3rd and 5th. It looks like a styling phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Hair gel is a styling product, a treatment applied to hair.

clue.text: Loses control of scud missile successfully

parts.note: to scud is to run or move fast
a SAM is a surface-to-air missile
OK means all right, done successfully

explanation.surface: A military report says a Scud missile struck its target.
explanation.walkthrough: 'scud' looks like the Scud missile, but here it is the verb meaning to race along.
explanation.definitionFit: To run amok is to behave wildly and out of control.

indicators.note: apparently says the name is there to be seen in the words that follow, on show in plain sight

parts.note: the letters of the saint's name read as '..., as if the martyr were to go on living

explanation.surface: An Italian martyr seems to be going to survive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'apparently' shows the saint's name running through "martyr's to live"; 'martyr' does double duty as part of the definition, a liberty the blog also notes. St Olive of Palermo was a young Sicilian martyr.
explanation.definitionFit: St Olive of Palermo was a young Christian martyr from Sicily, an Italian saint.

parts.note: in football the match official decides whether to award a penalty kick

explanation.surface: A court judge is meant to set the sentence.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a court sentence, but the penalty is a penalty kick in football, awarded by the match official.
explanation.definitionFit: A referee is the official who judges a sporting match and decides on penalties.
